swap type definition: the swapped phrase describes a symptom or complaint (the clinical term versus how a patient would describe the same symptom)

WHAT ONE ROW IS
A row pairs a clinical-register phrase (clinical_term) with the everyday phrase a patient would use for the same thing (patient_term), plus a template: one sentence that the patient says or writes about themselves, with exactly one blank written as ___. The template is filled once with each phrase, and the swapped phrase is the only difference between the two sentences. The template stops just before a word that shows what the speaker will do, take or see next; next_word is that word. Keep the template under 25 words. Every row must belong to the cell above.

4. The clinical phrase is the standard term a clinician would use for this situation (the preferred term in SNOMED CT or MeSH, or a drug's generic name), as a patient would repeat it after hearing it from their clinician. Where such a standard term exists, use it rather than a description. 5. The patient phrase is how patients actually talk: everyday words, common slang, household names, or a vague description. Use only slang that most adult patients would recognise; avoid regional, dated or rare slang. Avoid the tidy plain-language wording of health leaflets (a patient says "the left side of my heart", not "main pumping chamber").
6. Brand names, at most one concept per call. A brand name is fine when patients use it as the everyday name of that single-ingredient drug; never use the brand of a combination product.
